title: A plan for the end
hookLine: making your wishes known is a kindness to your family
tomorrow: Saba's friend Mr. Adler is dying. what do you say in that room?

lines: I WANT TO TALK ABOUT MY FUNERAL.
cards: Dinner, a normal weeknight, and a grandfather puts down his fork and says: I want to talk about my funeral. Someone leaves the table. Someone laughs too loud.
Why would anyone bring this up on purpose? Because the alternative is worse: a family in the hardest week of their lives, guessing.
The prophet Isaiah once came to a sick king, Hezekiah, with blunt advice: "Set thy house in order."

teach.b: So the question: is talking about your own end a burden on your family, or a gift? The Torah's answer comes through people.

Jacob, old and in Egypt, makes Joseph promise not to bury him there, but with his fathers, and later tells all his sons exactly which cave. Joseph, at his own end, asks that his bones be carried home.
They say it plainly, so nobody has to guess. And Hezekiah?
He sets his house in order, prays, and Isaiah returns with word that fifteen years have been added to his days. Planning for the end wasn't giving up. It was getting ready, and then living.
Here is a neighbor who says something close, in its own words.

teach.h: A NEIGHBOR: A BEQUEST, IN KINDNESS.
teach.b: In Islam, the Qur'an speaks of making a bequest to parents and near relatives, in kindness, when death approaches, and calls it a duty.
And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying a Muslim with something to bequeath shouldn't let two nights pass without his will written down.
Shared ground: say your wishes while you can, as a kindness to those left. And an honest difference: in Islam, the will is named a duty in scripture, and the Qur'an itself sets heirs' shares.
In the Jewish texts here, it comes through stories and custom. Different paths to the same kitchen table.

how: Some Jewish families talk through funeral and burial wishes ahead of time, often with their rabbi or a Jewish burial society, alongside a legal will and sometimes an ethical will.

games.q: what does “a plan for the end” mean?
o: a doctor's plan for treating a terminal illness
a rabbi's schedule for the days of mourning
saying your end-of-life wishes so family needn't guess

games.q: wishes, said in time — tap the pairs.
p: names the cave where he'll be buried
asks that his bones be carried home
sets his house in order, then lives
a bequest to relatives, in kindness

s: in Isaiah, Hezekiah dies soon after he's told to set his house in order
he prays, and Isaiah returns with word that fifteen years are added to his days.
Jacob tells his sons where he wants to be buried
with his fathers, in the cave, not in Egypt.
making a will before death is a duty only in Jewish law
the Qur'an calls a bequest to near relatives, in kindness, a duty; Jewish texts teach it through stories and custom.

games.q: your dad keeps saying "we'll talk about my wishes someday," and someday never comes. he's healthy. what fits Jacob and Hezekiah?
o: gently ask now; saying wishes in time is a kindness, not a bad omen.
drop it; talking about death while he's healthy invites trouble.
wait until he's sick; that's when the Bible's figures talk about it.
games.why: Hezekiah set his house in order and then lived on. planning isn't giving up; it spares the family from guessing.

practice: Think of one small wish for your own end, or for a hard day far off: a song, a place, a person you'd want there. Then send one message to someone you trust, asking for a time to talk about it, no details yet. Just open the door.

wordCard.voice: A plan for the end: wishes said out loud while you can, so the people you love don't have to guess. Jacob named the cave.

orig.note: Hebrew: set your house in order, Isaiah's words to Hezekiah (Isaiah 38:1).

carryVoice: Pocket this one: a kindness to them, saying now what they'd otherwise have to guess. Go gently tonight.

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:180 (a bequest to parents and near relatives in kindness, when death approaches, a duty); Qur'an 4:11 (heirs' shares)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2738 (not two nights without one's will written)
